Variational autoencoders

A generator with fewer random inputs than pixels has no probability density over images. How can one still be trained by maximum likelihood?

Nov 2, 2026 49 min read PDF
Contents
  • Autoencoders
  • From autoencoder to generator
  • A generator with a density
  • The evidence lower bound
  • Reconstruction and regularization
  • Training
  • The latent space
  • When it fails
  • Where the blur comes from
  • Summary

You will learn

  • Why a network that compresses and rebuilds images does not produce new ones when we feed it random numbers.
  • How a little noise gives a generator a probability for every image, and why that probability is still out of reach.
  • How a lower bound on that probability lets us train anyway, and how far it falls short on handwritten digits.
  • How the training loss splits into two terms that pull against each other, and how a gradient passes through a random draw.
  • What the trained model does with its inputs, where it fails and why its samples come out blurry.

Before you start

  • The pushforward, the manifold hypothesis and why generators have no density (Chapter 1)
  • Gibbs’ inequality, maximum likelihood as KL, upper and lower surrogates and the two directions of KL (Chapter 2)
  • Multivariate Gaussians and their covariance matrices, for the linear model
Code and results

A network can be trained to copy an image from its input to its output. Copying sounds pointless until we force the image through a narrow middle layer, only a few numbers wide. The first half of the network then has to shrink the image to those few numbers, and the second half has to rebuild the image from them.

Look at the second half on its own. It takes a few numbers and returns an image, which is what a generator does. So perhaps we already have a generator, and all it needs is random numbers as input.

We can try this. We train such a network on handwritten digits with 888 numbers in the middle, draw 888 random numbers 1,0001{,}0001,000 times and pass them to the second half. A digit classifier recognizes only 333 of the resulting images.

The same network rebuilds digits it has never seen, so its second half can produce digits when it receives the right numbers. Random numbers are rarely the right ones. This chapter is about how to train the network so that they are, which leads to the variational autoencoder (VAE) (Kingma and Welling 2014; Rezende, Mohamed, and Wierstra 2014).

Autoencoders

The network of the opening is called an autoencoder. The figure below shows one trained on handwritten digits, copying its input to its output through a narrow middle layer.

Definition 1 (Autoencoder). An autoencoder is a pair of maps. The encoder e:Rd→Rke : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^ke:Rd→Rk turns an image xxx into a code z=e(x)z = e(x)z=e(x), and the decoder g:Rk→Rdg : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^dg:Rk→Rd turns a code back into an image x^=g(e(x))\widehat{x} = g(e(x))x=g(e(x)), with k<dk < dk<d. Given training images X1,…,XnX_1, \dots, X_nX1​,…,Xn​, both are trained to minimize the reconstruction error 1n∑i=1n∥g(e(Xi))−Xi∥2. \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big\| g(e(X_i)) - X_i \big\|^2 . n1​i=1∑n​​g(e(Xi​))−Xi​​2.

A code as long as the image could hold every pixel, and the networks could simply pass it through. A code of 888 numbers cannot, so training pushes the encoder to keep the information that most reduces the reconstruction error, and the decoder rebuilds the image from what was kept.

What the autoencoder learns depends on how flexible eee and ggg are, and the two extremes show the range. If both are affine maps (linear plus a constant), the best autoencoder projects the data onto the span of its first kkk principal components (Baldi and Hornik 1989), so a nonlinear autoencoder generalizes principal component analysis. If both are very flexible, they can reach zero error on the training set by memorizing it, with the encoder sending the iii-th training image to the number iii and the decoder sending iii back to the iii-th image. This is the copying model of Chapter 1 again.

It may seem odd that 888 numbers can describe a 784784784-pixel digit, but this is what Chapter 1 would lead us to expect. Digits concentrate near a manifold (Chapter 1, Assumption 5) whose dimension Pope et al. (2021) estimate between 777 and 131313. The decoder parametrizes that manifold, since g(z)g(z)g(z) moves along it as zzz moves, and the encoder gives coordinates that locate an image on it. A code of 888 numbers sits at the low end of that range, so it keeps the main factors of variation and loses the rest, as the reconstruction above shows.

From autoencoder to generator

If the decoder moves along the surface where digits live, the obvious way to generate a digit is to pick a code at random and decode it. We draw the code from N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I), the distribution γ\gammaγ of Chapter 1, which from now on we call the prior. Codes drawn this way almost never give a digit, as the measurements at the end of this section show.

The trouble is that the decoder was trained only on the nnn codes of the training images, and nothing in the training controls where these codes lie. A code drawn from the prior may fall far from all of them and decode into a blend of digits or into nothing recognizable. Fitting a single Gaussian to the codes after training does not solve this, because the Gaussian still puts mass between the codes, where the decoder is untrained.

So a decoder that generates needs two properties of the code space that the autoencoder never asked for. Small moves of the code should give small changes of the image, including between the codes of training images, where a plain autoencoder’s decoder is unconstrained. Every code that the prior may produce should also decode into a plausible image. The VAE works towards both with two changes to the autoencoder, and the first replaces each code by a small cloud of codes.

Definition 2 (Gaussian encoder). A Gaussian encoder is a neural network that maps an image xxx to a mean μ(x)∈Rk\mu(x) \in \mathbb{R}^kμ(x)∈Rk and standard deviations σ(x)∈(0,+∞)k\sigma(x) \in (0, +\infty)^kσ(x)∈(0,+∞)k. It defines the distribution of codes q(z∣x)=N(μ(x),diag⁡(σ(x)2)). q(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu(x), \operatorname{diag}(\sigma(x)^2)\big). q(z∣x)=N(μ(x),diag(σ(x)2)).

During training the code of xxx is drawn from q(z∣x)q(z \mid x)q(z∣x), and the decoder must rebuild xxx from whichever code comes out, so every code near the centre of the cloud must decode into something close to xxx. That gives us the first property inside one cloud. The clouds also connect the images to each other. Where the clouds of two images overlap, the decoder must produce something between the two images, so it is trained on the space between training codes as well.

Clouds alone are not enough, because the encoder could shrink σ(x)\sigma(x)σ(x) to zero and fall back to a plain autoencoder, or push the clouds far apart so that they never overlap. The second change is aimed at the second property. It adds to the loss a term that grows when q(z∣x)q(z \mid x)q(z∣x) moves away from N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I), the KL divergence from the cloud to the prior, whose formula we derive later. The reconstruction term favours small and well-separated clouds, while the penalty favours clouds that look like the prior. At the balance between the two terms, the clouds move into the region where the prior puts its mass while still telling images apart. With a code of 222 numbers they nearly fill that region. With 888 numbers there is far more room to fill, and we return to this when the model fails.

To see what each term does, we train the same architecture three ways. If the two changes work, the codes of the VAE should spread over the disk of the prior, and random codes should decode into digits.

With reconstruction only, the codes spread far beyond the prior. The prior’s disk covers only the crowded centre where classes overlap, and prior codes decode into faint blends. With both terms the classes spread over the prior’s disk and the same five codes decode into digits, although the count below shows that many other codes do not. When the penalty dominates, most coordinates of the code collapse onto the prior. The code then carries almost no information, and prior codes decode into a few nearly identical blurred shapes.

The figure shows only five samples, so we count. If nearly every prior code decoded into a clear digit, the share recognized would come close to that of real digits.

Lab

What the two terms do, measured

We decode 1,0001{,}0001,000 codes drawn from N(0,I8)\mathcal{N}(0, I_8)N(0,I8​) with each 888-dimensional model. A fixed digit classifier with 98.9%98.9\%98.9% test accuracy, used throughout the course, says whether it recognizes a digit with more than 90%90\%90% confidence.

Images Recognized as a digit
plain autoencoder, prior codes 0.3%
VAE, prior codes 46.7%
VAE whose penalty dominates, prior codes 15.1%
real test digits (all 10,000) 96.8%

The codes of the plain autoencoder with k=2k = 2k=2 have standard deviations of 5.85.85.8 and 4.34.34.3 where the prior has 111. Of these codes, 95%95\%95% lie within radius 16.716.716.7, against 2.452.452.45 for the prior. The balanced VAE’s clouds have an average standard deviation of 0.050.050.05 and a KL to the prior of 24.824.824.8 nats per image. In the model whose penalty dominates, 666 of the 888 coordinates of the code no longer vary across images, the clouds have an average standard deviation of 0.920.920.92 and their KL to the prior is 0.830.830.83 nats. Retraining the classifier moved the recognized shares by up to about one percentage point in two retrainings. Each model was trained once, with one seed.

The two changes lift the share from 0.3%0.3\%0.3% to 46.7%46.7\%46.7%, about half of what real digits reach, and a heavier penalty brings it back down to 15.1%15.1\%15.1%. So the balance matters. We chose both changes because they looked sensible, and nothing so far tells us why this penalty is the right one or how much of it to use. The next section starts from a different problem, and its solution answers both questions.

A generator with a density

Chapter 2 ended with an obstacle. Maximum likelihood needs a density, and a generator with fewer latent dimensions than pixels has none. Chapter 1 sketched the repair, which is to add a little Gaussian noise to the output, and we now ask what that lets us compute. We start from the simplest generator we can draw, a line in the plane with noise around it. With k=1k = 1k=1 and d=2d = 2d=2, take a vector a∈R2a \in \mathbb{R}^2a∈R2 and a point b∈R2b \in \mathbb{R}^2b∈R2 and draw X=aZ+b+σdec ε,Z∼N(0,1),ε∼N(0,I2), X = aZ + b + \sigma_{\text{dec}}\, \varepsilon, \qquad Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_2), X=aZ+b+σdec​ε,Z∼N(0,1),ε∼N(0,I2​), with ZZZ and ε\varepsilonε independent. Without the noise every sample lies on the line {az+b:z∈R}\{az + b : z \in \mathbb{R}\}{az+b:z∈R}, which has zero area, and the distribution has no density. With the noise the samples form a band around the line. The point XXX is then Gaussian with mean bbb and covariance aa⊤+σdec2I2aa^\top + \sigma^2_{\text{dec}} I_2aa⊤+σdec2​I2​, the sum of the covariances of aZaZaZ and of the noise, and its density is positive everywhere in the plane.

The noise also lets us ask something new of the model, which is the set of codes that could have produced a given point xxx. The right panel shows them, and this is the object the rest of the chapter turns on. Codes whose point az+baz + baz+b lies near xxx are likely, so they form a narrow Gaussian over zzz when the noise is small.

The same construction works for any generator. A Gaussian decoder with variance σdec2>0\sigma^2_{\text{dec}} > 0σdec2​>0 turns a code zzz into the distribution N(gθ(z),σdec2Id)\mathcal{N}\big(g_\theta(z), \sigma^2_{\text{dec}} I_d\big)N(gθ​(z),σdec2​Id​), centred on the output of a network gθ:Rk→Rdg_\theta : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^dgθ​:Rk→Rd with weights θ\thetaθ. From now on we write p(z)p(z)p(z) for the density of the prior and pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x \mid z)pθ​(x∣z) for the density of this Gaussian. The model draws ZZZ from the prior and then XXX from pθ(⋅∣Z)p_\theta(\cdot \mid Z)pθ​(⋅∣Z). To find how likely an image is, we go through every code, ask how likely that code is to produce the image and weight the answer by how likely the code is, so XXX has the density pθ(x)=∫Rkpθ(x∣z) p(z) dz, p_\theta(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^k} p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz , pθ​(x)=∫Rk​pθ​(x∣z)p(z)dz, a mixture of Gaussians with one component for every code.

This density is what maximum likelihood was missing. It lies between 000 and (2πσdec2)−d/2(2\pi\sigma^2_{\text{dec}})^{-d/2}(2πσdec2​)−d/2 at every image, and the log-likelihood has a finite average over the data when the images and the decoder outputs have finite second moments (Proposition 3). Chapter 2’s result on maximum likelihood asks for exactly this finite average, so maximizing the average log-likelihood of the noisy model minimizes an estimate of KL(P∗ ∥ Pθ)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^* \,\|\, \mathbb{P}_\theta)KL(P∗∥Pθ​) up to a constant.

We should flag one simplification before going on. The images we display are decoder means gθ(Z)g_\theta(Z)gθ​(Z). The guarantees of the chapter concern the noisy model, and the displayed images come from a different distribution that the likelihood does not score.

The evidence lower bound

Maximum likelihood asks for log⁡pθ(Xi)\log p_\theta(X_i)logpθ​(Xi​) for every training image, and each one is an integral over Rk\mathbb{R}^kRk. We reach a usable target in three steps. We try the plainest estimate of the integral and see it fail. We improve it with the encoder. We then turn it into a lower bound that can be estimated and differentiated from one code per image, and whose gap to the log-likelihood has an exact form.

Why sampling the prior fails

The integral is an average over the prior, so the plainest estimate draws codes from the prior and averages pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x \mid z)pθ​(x∣z). This estimates pθ(x)p_\theta(x)pθ​(x) without bias, and on MNIST it is useless. For each of 100100100 test digits we drew 100,000100{,}000100,000 codes from the prior and decoded them with the 888-dimensional VAE of this chapter. For the median digit a single code carried essentially all of the weight, and the estimate of log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) was 858585 nats below the one obtained with the encoder in the next subsection. I expected prior sampling to be noisy. I did not expect one code out of 100,000100{,}000100,000 to carry nearly all the weight.

The region of good codes is tiny, and the Gaussian decoder punishes everything outside it. With σdec2=0.03\sigma^2_{\text{dec}} = 0.03σdec2​=0.03, two decoded images whose squared errors to xxx differ by 333 differ in pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x \mid z)pθ​(x∣z) by a factor exp⁡(3/0.06)=exp⁡(50)\exp(3 / 0.06) = \exp(50)exp(3/0.06)=exp(50), and the codes that decode close to a given digit fill a tiny part of the prior’s mass.

The linear model shows how this scales, since there the number of prior codes needed for a given precision can be computed exactly (Proposition 5), and it grows geometrically with the latent dimension. With k=8k = 8k=8 latent coordinates and the noise level of our VAE, a relative error of 10%10\%10% needs at least 9×1069 \times 10^69×106 prior codes for a single image, and every coordinate added multiplies this by at least 4.24.24.2.

Importance sampling with the encoder

Prior sampling fails because almost every code it draws is a bad one for this image. The natural repair is to draw codes from a distribution that favours the good ones, and the linear model shows how far this can go. There the posterior is known, and drawing the codes from it makes every sample give the exact answer.

Drawing from a different distribution changes the average, so we need a correction. This is importance sampling. It estimates an expectation under one distribution with samples from another distribution called the proposal, and it corrects each sample by a weight. With a proposal q(z)q(z)q(z) that is positive wherever p(z)p(z)p(z) is, the weight w(z)=pθ(x∣z) p(z)/q(z)w(z) = p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z) / q(z)w(z)=pθ​(x∣z)p(z)/q(z) satisfies pθ(x)=∫q(z) pθ(x∣z) p(z)q(z) dz=Ez∼q[w(z)]. p_\theta(x) = \int q(z)\, \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q(z)}\, dz = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q}\big[w(z)\big]. pθ​(x)=∫q(z)q(z)pθ​(x∣z)p(z)​dz=Ez∼q​[w(z)]. The ratio p(z)/q(z)p(z) / q(z)p(z)/q(z) makes the correction. A code that the proposal draws more often than the prior would is scaled down, and one it draws less often is scaled up. With the prior itself as proposal the ratio is 111, and we are back to the estimate of the last subsection. Each proposal gives the right average, so what separates them is how much the weights vary.

Proposition 6 (The posterior is the best proposal). For every proposal qqq positive wherever p(z)p(z)p(z) is, the weight w(Z)w(Z)w(Z) with Z∼qZ \sim qZ∼q has mean pθ(x)p_\theta(x)pθ​(x). Its variance is zero if and only if qqq is the posterior pθ(z∣x)p_\theta(z \mid x)pθ​(z∣x), and then w(z)=pθ(x)w(z) = p_\theta(x)w(z)=pθ​(x) for every zzz.

Proof.

The mean is the identity above. Bayes’ rule gives pθ(x∣z) p(z)=pθ(z∣x) pθ(x)p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z) = p_\theta(z \mid x)\, p_\theta(x)pθ​(x∣z)p(z)=pθ​(z∣x)pθ​(x), so w(z)=pθ(x) pθ(z∣x)/q(z)w(z) = p_\theta(x)\, p_\theta(z \mid x) / q(z)w(z)=pθ​(x)pθ​(z∣x)/q(z). If qqq is the posterior, w(z)=pθ(x)w(z) = p_\theta(x)w(z)=pθ​(x) for every zzz and the variance is zero. Conversely, a variance of zero means that w(Z)w(Z)w(Z) equals its mean pθ(x)p_\theta(x)pθ​(x) with probability 111. Then pθ(z∣x)=q(z)p_\theta(z \mid x) = q(z)pθ​(z∣x)=q(z) for qqq-almost every zzz, and since both are densities that integrate to 111, they are equal as distributions.

So the ideal proposal is the posterior, the one distribution we cannot write down for a neural decoder. We do have something close at hand. The Gaussian encoder already produces a cloud of codes for each image, and that cloud can serve as the proposal. If it is trained to come close to pθ(z∣x)p_\theta(z \mid x)pθ​(z∣x), which the bound below will arrange, it deserves the name approximate posterior qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x).

On MNIST it is a much better proposal than the prior. The 858585 nats of the last subsection compare 1,0001{,}0001,000 codes from the encoder of each test digit with 100,000100{,}000100,000 codes from the prior, for the median digit. The weights still vary a lot. Their effective number (∑iwi)2/∑iwi2(\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2(∑i​wi​)2/∑i​wi2​ is 2.42.42.4 out of 1,0001{,}0001,000 for the median digit, so only a few codes count.

The bound

We now have a way to estimate the likelihood of an image. We draw codes from the encoder, compute the weight w(z)w(z)w(z) of each one and average the weights. For training this is still not what we need. Training maximizes the logarithm of the likelihood, so the quantity to estimate is log⁡E[w]\log \mathbb{E}[w]logE[w], the logarithm of an average. The average of a few weights is an unbiased estimate of E[w]\mathbb{E}[w]E[w]. Its logarithm is a biased estimate of log⁡E[w]\log \mathbb{E}[w]logE[w], and its gradient is biased too.

To make progress we swap the two operations. We take the logarithm of each weight first and average afterwards. With a single code this gives log⁡w(z)\log w(z)logw(z), which we can compute and differentiate directly. The swap changes the value, and we can say in which direction. The logarithm is concave, so Jensen’s inequality gives log⁡E[w]≥E[log⁡w]\log \mathbb{E}[w] \ge \mathbb{E}[\log w]logE[w]≥E[logw]. The new quantity therefore never exceeds the log-likelihood, which makes it a lower bound. A lower bound is a useful training target only if it stays close to what it bounds, so we also need the size of the gap. The theorem gives both.

Theorem 7 (Evidence lower bound). For every image xxx and every density qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x), log⁡pθ(x)≥Lθ,ϕ(x)=Ez∼qϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z) p(z)qϕ(z∣x)]. \log p_\theta(x) \ge \mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(x) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)}\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\right]. logpθ​(x)≥Lθ,ϕ​(x)=Ez∼qϕ​(z∣x)​[logqϕ​(z∣x)pθ​(x∣z)p(z)​]. The gap is exactly a KL divergence, log⁡pθ(x)−Lθ,ϕ(x)=KL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ pθ(z∣x))\log p_\theta(x) - \mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(x) = \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big)logpθ​(x)−Lθ,ϕ​(x)=KL(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x)). The quantity Lθ,ϕ(x)\mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(x)Lθ,ϕ​(x) is the evidence lower bound (ELBO).

Proof.

Bayes’ rule gives pθ(x∣z) p(z)=pθ(z∣x) pθ(x)p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z) = p_\theta(z \mid x)\, p_\theta(x)pθ​(x∣z)p(z)=pθ​(z∣x)pθ​(x) for every zzz. Substituting it inside the logarithm, Lθ,ϕ(x)=Eq[log⁡pθ(x)+log⁡pθ(z∣x)qϕ(z∣x)]=log⁡pθ(x)−Eq[log⁡qϕ(z∣x)pθ(z∣x)]=log⁡pθ(x)−KL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ pθ(z∣x)), \mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(x) = \mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\log p_\theta(x) + \log \frac{p_\theta(z \mid x)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\right] = \log p_\theta(x) - \mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\log \frac{q_\phi(z \mid x)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)}\right] = \log p_\theta(x) - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big), Lθ,ϕ​(x)=Eq​[logpθ​(x)+logqϕ​(z∣x)pθ​(z∣x)​]=logpθ​(x)−Eq​[logpθ​(z∣x)qϕ​(z∣x)​]=logpθ​(x)−KL(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x)), where the first term leaves the expectation because it does not depend on zzz. By Gibbs’ inequality the gap is non-negative, and it vanishes exactly when the encoder equals the true posterior.

Take the gap formula first. Its left side is how far the bound falls short for this image, and its right side says the shortfall is the KL from the encoder’s cloud to the true posterior, so the bound is exact when the two coincide and loose when the encoder misses. Two extreme encoders show the range. If qϕq_\phiqϕ​ is the posterior, every weight equals pθ(x)p_\theta(x)pθ​(x) by Proposition 6, the swap of logarithm and average changes nothing and the gap is 000. If qϕq_\phiqϕ​ is the prior for every image, the ELBO becomes Ez∼p(z)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)]Ez∼p(z)​[logpθ​(x∣z)], and the gap is the KL from the wide prior to a posterior that the figure of the linear model shows can be far narrower.

The ELBO is the expected logarithm of the importance weight, Lθ,ϕ(x)=Eq[log⁡w]\mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(x) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log w]Lθ,ϕ​(x)=Eq​[logw], while the log-likelihood is the logarithm of its expectation. Unlike the log-likelihood it contains only things we can evaluate, namely the decoder, the prior and the encoder. The posterior that we could not compute appears only in the gap, which we never have to evaluate.

The VAE maximizes the ELBO jointly in θ\thetaθ and ϕ\phiϕ. The log-likelihood does not depend on ϕ\phiϕ, so raising the ELBO in ϕ\phiϕ can only close the gap. This is what trains the encoder to approach the posterior. Raising it in θ\thetaθ can raise the likelihood or close the gap, and we return to this below.

What the bound costs

The theorem speaks about one image, while training averages over all of them. To compare that average with the distance of Chapter 2, it helps to look at an image and its code together, as a pair. There are two ways to produce such a pair, and the average of the negative bound turns out to compare them. Up to the constant Elog⁡p∗(X)\mathbb{E}\log p^*(X)Elogp∗(X), it is a KL divergence between the two, and this gives its exact relation to the distance. The data and the encoder define one distribution of pairs, which draws an image X∼P∗X \sim \mathbb{P}^*X∼P∗ and then a code from qϕ(⋅∣X)q_\phi(\cdot \mid X)qϕ​(⋅∣X). The model defines another, which draws a code from the prior and then an image from the decoder.

Proposition 8 (The negative ELBO is a joint KL). Let P∗\mathbb{P}^*P∗ have a density p∗p^*p∗ with E∣log⁡p∗(X)∣<∞\mathbb{E}|\log p^*(X)| < \inftyE∣logp∗(X)∣<∞, let qϕ(x,z)=p∗(x) qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(x, z) = p^*(x)\, q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(x,z)=p∗(x)qϕ​(z∣x) and pθ(x,z)=p(z) pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x, z) = p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)pθ​(x,z)=p(z)pθ​(x∣z), and assume the expectations below are finite. Then KL(qϕ(x,z) ∥ pθ(x,z))=− EX∼P∗[Lθ,ϕ(X)]+EX∼P∗[log⁡p∗(X)]=KL(P∗ ∥ Pθ)+EX∼P∗ KL(qϕ(⋅∣X) ∥ pθ(⋅∣X)). \begin{aligned} \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(x, z) \,\|\, p_\theta(x, z)\big) &= -\,\mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mathbb{P}^*}\big[\mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(X)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mathbb{P}^*}\big[\log p^*(X)\big] \\ &= \mathrm{KL}\big(\mathbb{P}^* \,\|\, \mathbb{P}_\theta\big) + \mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mathbb{P}^*}\, \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\cdot \mid X) \,\|\, p_\theta(\cdot \mid X)\big). \end{aligned} KL(qϕ​(x,z)∥pθ​(x,z))​=−EX∼P∗​[Lθ,ϕ​(X)]+EX∼P∗​[logp∗(X)]=KL(P∗∥Pθ​)+EX∼P∗​KL(qϕ​(⋅∣X)∥pθ​(⋅∣X)).​

Proof.

By definition, KL(qϕ(x,z) ∥ pθ(x,z))=E(X,Z)∼qϕ[log⁡qϕ(X,Z)−log⁡pθ(X,Z)]\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(x, z) \,\|\, p_\theta(x, z)) = \mathbb{E}_{(X, Z) \sim q_\phi}\big[\log q_\phi(X, Z) - \log p_\theta(X, Z)\big]KL(qϕ​(x,z)∥pθ​(x,z))=E(X,Z)∼qϕ​​[logqϕ​(X,Z)−logpθ​(X,Z)]. KL(qϕ​(x,z)∥pθ​(x,z))=EX​[logp∗(X)]+EX​EZ∼qϕ​(⋅∣X)​[logp(Z)pθ​(X∣Z)qϕ​(Z∣X)​]. The inner expectation is −Lθ,ϕ(X)-\mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(X)−Lθ,ϕ​(X), which gives the first equality. For the second, Theorem 7 gives for each XXX −Lθ,ϕ(X)=−log⁡pθ(X)+KL(qϕ(⋅∣X) ∥ pθ(⋅∣X)), -\mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(X) = -\log p_\theta(X) + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\cdot \mid X) \,\|\, p_\theta(\cdot \mid X)\big), −Lθ,ϕ​(X)=−logpθ​(X)+KL(qϕ​(⋅∣X)∥pθ​(⋅∣X)), and E[log⁡p∗(X)]−E[log⁡pθ(X)]=KL(P∗ ∥ Pθ)\mathbb{E}[\log p^*(X)] - \mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(X)] = \mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^* \,\|\, \mathbb{P}_\theta)E[logp∗(X)]−E[logpθ​(X)]=KL(P∗∥Pθ​) by Chapter 2, Proposition 9.

Read the second line of the proposition from left to right. For the two distributions of pairs to agree, the images have to agree and so do the codes of each image. The first term measures the images and the second measures the codes. The proposition assumes that the data have a density, which is compatible with Chapter 1, since data that concentrate near a manifold can still have one.

In the language of Chapters 1 and 2, the distance of the VAE is R(θ)=KL(P∗ ∥ Pθ)R(\theta) = \mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^* \,\|\, \mathbb{P}_\theta)R(θ)=KL(P∗∥Pθ​), the direction of maximum likelihood. Its surrogate is the averaged negative ELBO, which equals the joint KL above up to the constant Elog⁡p∗(X)\mathbb{E}\log p^*(X)Elogp∗(X) and is estimated on the training images. The gap is the average KL from the encoder to the posterior, and it is never negative, so the surrogate is an upper bound on the distance. This is the safe side of Chapter 2, where driving the surrogate down also drives the distance down.

We can now write what the bound costs. Give each decoder its best encoder and write gap(θ)\text{gap}(\theta)gap(θ) for the average KL that remains. Let θ^\widehat{\theta}θ be the decoder that minimizes the surrogate. Then Chapter 2’s proposition on upper and lower surrogates gives R(θ^)≤R(θ)+gap(θ)R(\widehat{\theta}) \le R(\theta) + \text{gap}(\theta)R(θ)≤R(θ)+gap(θ) for every θ\thetaθ, so the trained decoder is as good as any other decoder up to that decoder’s gap. Optimizing ϕ\phiϕ only shrinks the gap. Optimizing θ\thetaθ can also shrink it by making the posterior easier to approximate, so the bound favours decoders whose posteriors look like diagonal Gaussians (Cremer, Li, and Duvenaud 2018).

The gap can also be measured, at least from below. We estimate log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) by the logarithm of the average weight of 1,0001{,}0001,000 encoder codes. The logarithm of an average falls below log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) on average by Jensen’s inequality, as the ELBO does. The difference between this estimate and the ELBO is therefore a lower bound on the gap, up to sampling noise. For the median test digit it is about 141414 nats, and the ELBO of that digit is about 468468468.

A positive log-likelihood may look wrong, but a density can exceed 111. Here the Gaussian decoder contributes the constant −d2log⁡(2πσdec2)≈+654-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}) \approx +654−2d​log(2πσdec2​)≈+654 nats. The average ELBO over the test set is lower than the median, about 654−212−25≈417654 - 212 - 25 \approx 417654−212−25≈417 nats, where we subtract the two parts of the loss that the next section separates.

In the linear model the gap can vanish, because the posterior of Proposition 4 has a mean linear in xxx and a fixed covariance, which a linear Gaussian encoder can match (a diagonal one when A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is diagonal).

Going furtherThree KL divergences, and the name of the method

Three KL divergences appear in a VAE. Maximum likelihood minimizes KL(P∗ ∥ Pθ)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^* \,\|\, \mathbb{P}_\theta)KL(P∗∥Pθ​) in image space, whose forward direction pushes the model to cover every mode of the data. The gap KL(qϕ ∥ pθ(z∣x))\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x))KL(qϕ​∥pθ​(z∣x)) lives in code space in the mode-seeking direction of Chapter 2’s lab, so a diagonal Gaussian encoder tends to underestimate the spread of a correlated posterior and to pick one mode of a posterior with several. The penalty KL(qϕ ∥ p(z))\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \,\|\, p(z))KL(qϕ​∥p(z)) of the next section pulls each cloud towards the prior.

The name of the method comes from the encoder. Finding the Gaussian (μ,σ)(\mu, \sigma)(μ,σ) that maximizes the ELBO of one image is an optimization over a family of distributions, which is what variational inference means. The encoder amortizes this work, since one network answers for every image in a single forward pass. The gap therefore has two parts (Cremer, Li, and Duvenaud 2018, sec. 3.1). The approximation gap exists because the best diagonal Gaussian is not the posterior, and the amortization gap because one network does not find the best Gaussian for every image.

In the linear model the ELBO has no local maxima that the likelihood lacks (Lucas et al. 2019).

Reconstruction and regularization

The bound is still one expectation with a ratio inside it. To train on it, and to compare it with what we did by hand earlier, we split it. The split is one line.

Proposition 9 (The two terms of the ELBO). Lθ,ϕ(x)=Ez∼qϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]−KL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z)). \mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(x) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\big). Lθ,ϕ​(x)=Ez∼qϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]−KL(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z)).

Proof.

Split the logarithm in the definition of Lθ,ϕ(x)\mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(x)Lθ,ϕ​(x) into log⁡pθ(x∣z)+log⁡(p(z)/qϕ(z∣x))\log p_\theta(x \mid z) + \log \big(p(z) / q_\phi(z \mid x)\big)logpθ​(x∣z)+log(p(z)/qϕ​(z∣x)). The expectation of the second part under qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x) is −KL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z))-\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z))−KL(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z)) by the definition of KL.

These are the reconstruction term and the penalty of the section “From autoencoder to generator”. We added them there because they looked sensible, and they now come out of the likelihood with nothing added. On MNIST the two have very different sizes. On the test set the KL from the encoder to the prior averages 24.824.824.8 nats per image, and the squared reconstruction error averages 12.712.712.7, which contributes 12.7/(2×0.03)≈21212.7 / (2 \times 0.03) \approx 21212.7/(2×0.03)≈212 nats.

That division by 2σdec22\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}2σdec2​ comes from the Gaussian decoder, whose log-density is log⁡pθ(x∣z)=−12σdec2∥x−gθ(z)∥2−d2log⁡(2πσdec2). \log p_\theta(x \mid z) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}} \|x - g_\theta(z)\|^2 - \frac{d}{2} \log\big(2\pi\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}\big). logpθ​(x∣z)=−2σdec2​1​∥x−gθ​(z)∥2−2d​log(2πσdec2​). With σdec2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}σdec2​ held fixed, the first term of the ELBO is therefore the reconstruction error of an autoencoder multiplied by −1/(2σdec2)-1/(2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}})−1/(2σdec2​), up to a constant. The second term has a closed form, which is the exact penalty we postponed.

Property 10 (KL between a Gaussian and the standard Gaussian). For μ∈Rk\mu \in \mathbb{R}^kμ∈Rk and σ∈(0,+∞)k\sigma \in (0, +\infty)^kσ∈(0,+∞)k, KL(N(μ,diag⁡(σ2)) ∥ N(0,I))=12∑j=1k(μj2+σj2−1−log⁡σj2). \mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \operatorname{diag}(\sigma^2)) \,\|\, \mathcal{N}(0, I)\big) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \big(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2\big). Each term vanishes exactly when μj=0\mu_j = 0μj​=0 and σj=1\sigma_j = 1σj​=1. The penalty grows when a cloud drifts from the origin and when it shrinks or spreads compared with the prior. Dropping constants and averaging over the training images, the VAE minimizes 1n∑i=1n(12σdec2 Ez∼qϕ(z∣Xi)∥Xi−gθ(z)∥2+12∑j=1k(μj(Xi)2+σj(Xi)2−1−log⁡σj(Xi)2)). \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \frac{1}{2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}}\, \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z \mid X_i)} \big\|X_i - g_\theta(z)\big\|^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \big(\mu_j(X_i)^2 + \sigma_j(X_i)^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j(X_i)^2\big) \right). n1​i=1∑n​(2σdec2​1​Ez∼qϕ​(z∣Xi​)​​Xi​−gθ​(z)​2+21​j=1∑k​(μj​(Xi​)2+σj​(Xi​)2−1−logσj​(Xi​)2)). This is an autoencoder loss with a noisy code and a penalty on the code distribution. The section “From autoencoder to generator” left open how much penalty to use. The formula now fixes the weight, which is set by the decoder variance. A small σdec2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}σdec2​ favours precise reconstructions and a large one favours codes close to the prior. The β\betaβ-VAE instead multiplies the KL term by a factor β>0\beta > 0β>0 (Higgins et al. 2017), and the next proposition shows that this amounts to changing the decoder variance.

Proposition 11 (The weight of the KL and the decoder variance). For every β>0\beta > 0β>0, the loss above with the KL term multiplied by β\betaβ has the same minimizers (θ,ϕ)(\theta, \phi)(θ,ϕ) as the loss with σdec2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}σdec2​ replaced by βσdec2\beta\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}βσdec2​ and no factor on the KL term.

Proof.

Multiplying a function by the positive constant 1/β1/\beta1/β does not change its minimizers. Applied to 12σdec2E∥X−gθ(Z)∥2+β KL\frac{1}{2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}} \mathbb{E}\|X - g_\theta(Z)\|^2 + \beta\, \mathrm{KL}2σdec2​1​E∥X−gθ​(Z)∥2+βKL, it gives 12βσdec2E∥X−gθ(Z)∥2+KL\frac{1}{2\beta\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}} \mathbb{E}\|X - g_\theta(Z)\|^2 + \mathrm{KL}2βσdec2​1​E∥X−gθ​(Z)∥2+KL, the loss with variance βσdec2\beta\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}βσdec2​.

So the weight on the KL and the decoder variance are one setting under two names. The likelihood can also choose this setting for us. For a single variance shared by all pixels the best value is the mean squared error per pixel, which is 0.0160.0160.016 on our 888-dimensional VAE, about half of the 0.030.030.03 we trained with. Training with that value changes little, as the fold-out below shows.

We can check how far our fixed choice is from this value. Our 888-dimensional VAE, trained with σdec2=0.03\sigma^2_{\text{dec}} = 0.03σdec2​=0.03, reaches a mean squared error of 0.0160.0160.016 per pixel on the test set. Training

Gradients of an expectation

Both terms of the loss are expectations over codes drawn from the encoder, and training needs their gradients. For the decoder’s weights this causes no difficulty, since they do not affect how the codes are drawn. The encoder’s weights do. Changing them changes the distribution the codes are drawn from, so the gradient cannot simply move inside the expectation. A general estimator exists for this case, the score-function (or REINFORCE) estimator. Its variance is high, almost four times that of the estimator below on the simplest example (Proposition 14).

The VAE takes another route, which is to separate the randomness from the weights. We draw fixed noise first and then let the encoder shift and scale it, so the code becomes a function of the noise.

Lemma 13 (Reparameterization). Let ε∼N(0,Ik)\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_k)ε∼N(0,Ik​) and z=μϕ(x)+σϕ(x)⊙εz = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilonz=μϕ​(x)+σϕ​(x)⊙ε, where ⊙\odot⊙ is the coordinate-wise product. Then z∼qϕ(z∣x)z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)z∼qϕ​(z∣x), and for every function uuu whose expectations exist Ez∼qϕ(z∣x)[u(z)]=Eε∼N(0,I)[u(μϕ(x)+σϕ(x)⊙ε)]. \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)}[u(z)] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\big[u\big(\mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon\big)\big]. Ez∼qϕ​(z∣x)​[u(z)]=Eε∼N(0,I)​[u(μϕ​(x)+σϕ​(x)⊙ε)]. If uuu is differentiable and ϕ↦u(μϕ(x)+σϕ(x)⊙ε)\phi \mapsto u(\mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon)ϕ↦u(μϕ​(x)+σϕ​(x)⊙ε) has a gradient bounded by an integrable function of ε\varepsilonε near each ϕ\phiϕ, the gradient in ϕ\phiϕ of the right-hand side is the expectation of the gradient of the integrand.

Proof.

Each coordinate zj=μj+σjεjz_j = \mu_j + \sigma_j \varepsilon_jzj​=μj​+σj​εj​ is an affine function of a standard Gaussian, so it is Gaussian with mean μj\mu_jμj​ and variance σj2\sigma_j^2σj2​. The coordinates are independent because the εj\varepsilon_jεj​ are. This is qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x), and the identity is the expectation of u(z)u(z)u(z) computed through the variable ε\varepsilonε that produces zzz. The exchange of gradient and expectation is the standard theorem of differentiation under the integral sign, which the domination assumption allows (dominated convergence).

On the right-hand side the distribution of ε\varepsilonε does not depend on ϕ\phiϕ, and ϕ\phiϕ only enters through a differentiable function. Under the conditions of the lemma the gradient can now move inside, and one draw of ε\varepsilonε gives an unbiased estimate of it. The code is now the pushforward of a fixed random variable by a map that depends on the parameters, as in Chapter 1.

Going furtherTwo gradient estimators

The difference between the two estimators already appears in one dimension. Two estimates of this derivative can be computed from one draw of ZZZ.

The first, the score-function (or REINFORCE) estimator, works for any distribution with a differentiable density qϕq_\phiqϕ​. Differentiating under the integral and writing ∇ϕqϕ=qϕ∇ϕlog⁡qϕ\nabla_\phi q_\phi = q_\phi \nabla_\phi \log q_\phi∇ϕ​qϕ​=qϕ​∇ϕ​logqϕ​, ∇ϕ Ez∼qϕ[u(z)]=∫u(z) ∇ϕqϕ(z) dz=Ez∼qϕ[u(z) ∇ϕlog⁡qϕ(z)], \nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi}[u(z)] = \int u(z)\, \nabla_\phi q_\phi(z)\, dz = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi}\big[u(z)\, \nabla_\phi \log q_\phi(z)\big], ∇ϕ​Ez∼qϕ​​[u(z)]=∫u(z)∇ϕ​qϕ​(z)dz=Ez∼qϕ​​[u(z)∇ϕ​logqϕ​(z)], so u(Z) ∇ϕlog⁡qϕ(Z)u(Z)\, \nabla_\phi \log q_\phi(Z)u(Z)∇ϕ​logqϕ​(Z) is an unbiased estimate. For the Gaussian, ∂μlog⁡q=(z−μ)/σ2\partial_\mu \log q = (z - \mu)/\sigma^2∂μ​logq=(z−μ)/σ2. Proposition 14 (Variance of the two estimators). For Z∼N(0,σ2)Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)Z∼N(0,σ2) and u(z)=z2u(z) = z^2u(z)=z2, both estimators of the derivative in μ\muμ at μ=0\mu = 0μ=0 have mean 000. The pathwise estimate 2Z2Z2Z has variance 4σ24\sigma^24σ2, and the score-function estimate Z3/σ2Z^3/\sigma^2Z3/σ2 has variance 15σ215\sigma^215σ2.

Proof.

At μ=0\mu = 0μ=0 the pathwise estimate is 2(0+σε)=2Z2(0 + \sigma\varepsilon) = 2Z2(0+σε)=2Z and the score-function estimate is Z2⋅Z/σ2=Z3/σ2Z^2 \cdot Z/\sigma^2 = Z^3/\sigma^2Z2⋅Z/σ2=Z3/σ2. Both have mean 000 because the odd moments of a centred Gaussian vanish. The variances are E[4Z2]=4σ2\mathbb{E}[4Z^2] = 4\sigma^2E[4Z2]=4σ2 and E[Z6]/σ4=15σ6/σ4=15σ2\mathbb{E}[Z^6]/\sigma^4 = 15\sigma^6/\sigma^4 = 15\sigma^2E[Z6]/σ4=15σ6/σ4=15σ2, using E[Z6]=15σ6\mathbb{E}[Z^6] = 15\sigma^6E[Z6]=15σ6 (the sixth moment of a centred Gaussian is 5⋅3⋅1 σ65 \cdot 3 \cdot 1\, \sigma^65⋅3⋅1σ6).

The score-function estimate ignores the shape of uuu and only weights its values, and its variance is almost four times larger in this simplest case. The VAE uses the pathwise estimate, which needs a continuous code and a differentiable decoder.

One code per image

A VAE draws one code per image at every step. Given how much the importance weights varied, this may seem too few, yet on MNIST it is enough for the gradient. For the median test digit, the logarithm of the importance weight of 1,0001{,}0001,000 encoder codes has a standard deviation of 6.76.76.7 nats. The weights themselves vary by a factor exp⁡(6.7)≈800\exp(6.7) \approx 800exp(6.7)≈800 between codes one standard deviation apart, which is why their effective number was 2.42.42.4. Working with the logarithm of the weights keeps the estimate stable. The single-code estimates of the ELBO and of its gradient are also unbiased, so their errors have no preferred direction, and they average out over the 128128128 images of a minibatch and over the steps.

The training step

One training step proceeds as follows.

  1. The encoder reads a minibatch and outputs μϕ(x)\mu_\phi(x)μϕ​(x) and log⁡σϕ(x)2\log \sigma_\phi(x)^2logσϕ​(x)2 (the logarithm keeps σ\sigmaσ positive without a constraint).
  2. The step draws ε∼N(0,Ik)\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_k)ε∼N(0,Ik​) for each image and forms z=μϕ(x)+σϕ(x)⊙εz = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilonz=μϕ​(x)+σϕ​(x)⊙ε.
  3. The decoder maps zzz to gθ(z)g_\theta(z)gθ​(z), and the loss adds the squared error divided by 2σdec22\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}2σdec2​ to the closed-form KL of Property 10.
  4. Backpropagation runs through the decoder, the code and the encoder, and an optimizer updates θ\thetaθ and ϕ\phiϕ.

In PyTorch the loss reads

def vae_loss(x, encoder, decoder, var_dec):
    mu, logvar = encoder(x)
    z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)   # reparameterization
    reconstruction = ((decoder(z) - x) ** 2).sum(dim=1) / (2 * var_dec)
    kl = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - 1 - logvar).sum(dim=1)
    return (reconstruction + kl).mean()

The main VAEs of this chapter have k=2k = 2k=2 or k=8k = 8k=8. Their encoders have layers of sizes 784→512→256→2784 \to 512 \to 256 \to 2784→512→256→2 and 784→256→64→8784 \to 256 \to 64 \to 8784→256→64→8, and their decoders mirror them. They were trained on MNIST with this loss and σdec2=0.03\sigma^2_{\text{dec}} = 0.03σdec2​=0.03, using Adam with learning rate 10−310^{-3}10−3 on batches of 128128128 for 303030 epochs. Other settings are given where they are used.

In practice

A learned decoder variance needs the term d2log⁡σdec2\frac{d}{2} \log \sigma^2_{\text{dec}}2d​logσdec2​ that the loss above drops, otherwise it grows without limit. A single shared variance then settles at the value of Proposition 12 (Rybkin, Daniilidis, and Levine 2021). A variance per pixel and per code is riskier, because a decoder that passes through one training image with a variance shrinking to zero there sends the likelihood to infinity (Mattei and Frellsen 2018).

Going furtherTwo more training tips

Binary cross-entropy, common as the reconstruction term on MNIST, is not a normalized density for grey pixels and biases the model. The continuous Bernoulli distribution corrects it (Loaiza-Ganem and Cunningham 2019).

Two tricks keep the optimizer from switching the code off before the decoder has learned to use it, which matters most with expressive decoders. One raises the weight of the KL term from 000 to 111 over the first epochs (Bowman et al. 2016). The other leaves the KL of each group of latent coordinates unpenalized below an allowance of a few nats (Kingma et al. 2016).

The latent space

We now have a trained model and can look at what it learned. With a code of k=2k = 2k=2 numbers we can see the decoder’s output over the whole latent plane.

For this 222-dimensional model almost every region where the prior puts mass decodes into a digit, and neighbouring codes decode into similar digits. These are the two properties we asked for when we first turned the autoencoder into a generator. Transitions between classes are gradual, and a 7 becomes a 9 through images that look like both. Moving along a straight line between two codes gives a smooth sequence of images, which is called interpolation in the latent space.

Going furtherDisentangled latent spaces

Directions in the latent plane also have a meaning. Along some of them the stroke tilts, and along others it thickens or one digit turns into another. A latent space is disentangled when each coordinate controls one such factor. The loss does not ask for this, and the prior cannot impose it, because N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I) does not change under rotations of the latent space. The diagonal covariance of the encoder breaks this symmetry and favours factors aligned with the axes (Rolinek, Zietlow, and Martius 2019). The β\betaβ-VAE strengthens this pressure with β>1\beta > 1β>1, and reconstructions then get blurrier (Higgins et al. 2017). Without such built-in preferences, unsupervised disentanglement cannot be guaranteed (Locatello et al. 2019).

The prior we chose in advance need not suit the encoder we ended up with, so we should ask which prior would. The answer is the distribution of all the codes. Drawing an image from the data and then a code from its cloud gives a code with the density qˉϕ(z)=EX∼P∗ qϕ(z∣X)\bar{q}_\phi(z) = \mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mathbb{P}^*}\, q_\phi(z \mid X)qˉ​ϕ​(z)=EX∼P∗​qϕ​(z∣X), the aggregate posterior. To compare it with the prior we take the average KL term of the loss, called the rate (a name from coding theory that the fold-out below explains), and split it into two parts. One is the mutual information Iq(x;z)=EX KL(qϕ(⋅∣X) ∥ qˉϕ)I_q(x; z) = \mathbb{E}_{X}\, \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\cdot \mid X) \,\|\, \bar{q}_\phi\big)Iq​(x;z)=EX​KL(qϕ​(⋅∣X)∥qˉ​ϕ​), the average number of nats a code tells about its image, and the other compares the codes as a whole with the prior.

Proposition 15 (The rate splits in two). EX∼P∗ KL(qϕ(⋅∣X) ∥ p)=Iq(x;z)+KL(qˉϕ ∥ p). \mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mathbb{P}^*}\, \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\cdot \mid X) \,\|\, p\big) = I_q(x; z) + \mathrm{KL}\big(\bar{q}_\phi \,\|\, p\big). EX∼P∗​KL(qϕ​(⋅∣X)∥p)=Iq​(x;z)+KL(qˉ​ϕ​∥p).

Proof.

Inside the KL, write log⁡qϕ(z∣x)p(z)=log⁡qϕ(z∣x)qˉϕ(z)+log⁡qˉϕ(z)p(z)\log \frac{q_\phi(z \mid x)}{p(z)} = \log \frac{q_\phi(z \mid x)}{\bar{q}_\phi(z)} + \log \frac{\bar{q}_\phi(z)}{p(z)}logp(z)qϕ​(z∣x)​=logqˉ​ϕ​(z)qϕ​(z∣x)​+logp(z)qˉ​ϕ​(z)​. Averaged over X∼P∗X \sim \mathbb{P}^*X∼P∗ and Z∼qϕ(⋅∣X)Z \sim q_\phi(\cdot \mid X)Z∼qϕ​(⋅∣X), the first part gives Iq(x;z)I_q(x; z)Iq​(x;z). The second part depends on zzz only, and the pair (X,Z)(X, Z)(X,Z) gives ZZZ the distribution qˉϕ\bar{q}_\phiqˉ​ϕ​, so its average is EZ∼qˉϕ[log⁡qˉϕ(Z)/p(Z)]=KL(qˉϕ ∥ p)\mathbb{E}_{Z \sim \bar{q}_\phi}[\log \bar{q}_\phi(Z) / p(Z)] = \mathrm{KL}(\bar{q}_\phi \,\|\, p)EZ∼qˉ​ϕ​​[logqˉ​ϕ​(Z)/p(Z)]=KL(qˉ​ϕ​∥p) (Hoffman and Johnson 2016).

Corollary 16 (The best prior is the aggregate posterior). For a fixed encoder and decoder, the prior density ppp that maximizes EX∼P∗[Lθ,ϕ(X)]\mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mathbb{P}^*}[\mathcal{L}_{\theta, \phi}(X)]EX∼P∗​[Lθ,ϕ​(X)] is qˉϕ\bar{q}_\phiqˉ​ϕ​.

Proof.

By Proposition 9 the prior enters the average ELBO only through the rate, with a minus sign. By Proposition 15 the rate is Iq(x;z)+KL(qˉϕ ∥ p)I_q(x; z) + \mathrm{KL}(\bar{q}_\phi \,\|\, p)Iq​(x;z)+KL(qˉ​ϕ​∥p), and IqI_qIq​ does not depend on ppp. By Gibbs’ inequality, KL(qˉϕ ∥ p)≥0\mathrm{KL}(\bar{q}_\phi \,\|\, p) \ge 0KL(qˉ​ϕ​∥p)≥0 with equality only at p=qˉϕp = \bar{q}_\phip=qˉ​ϕ​.

The fixed prior N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I) is therefore the right prior only when the codes of the data fill it. Where qˉϕ\bar{q}_\phiqˉ​ϕ​ puts little mass and the prior puts a lot, prior codes land where the decoder has seen few training codes. This leads directly to the first failure below.

Going furtherThe rate-distortion reading of the ELBO

Write the loss as −L=distortion+rate-\mathcal{L} = \text{distortion} + \text{rate}−L=distortion+rate, with the distortion −Elog⁡pθ(x∣z)-\mathbb{E}\log p_\theta(x \mid z)−Elogpθ​(x∣z) and the rate of Proposition 15, both in nats (Alemi et al. (2018) write them DDD and RRR). By Proposition 15 the rate bounds the information Iq(x;z)I_q(x; z)Iq​(x;z) in the code. Weighting the two terms as distortion+β⋅rate\text{distortion} + \beta \cdot \text{rate}distortion+β⋅rate moves along a trade-off curve between a precise code and a cheap one, and at an optimum the slope of the curve is −β-\beta−β (Alemi et al. 2018).

As β\betaβ falls from 100100100 to 0.10.10.1, the rate rises from 0.70.70.7 to 515151 nats per image. The squared error falls from 474747 to about 141414 and then stops improving. Repeating β=0.1\beta = 0.1β=0.1, 0.30.30.3 and 111 with three seeds gives squared errors between 14.014.014.0 and 14.614.614.6 for all three, so lowering β\betaβ below 111 adds rate without a measurable gain in squared error. In nats, the slope of the curve between β=3\beta = 3β=3 and β=1\beta = 1β=1 is −1.9-1.9−1.9, and between β=1\beta = 1β=1 and β=0.3\beta = 0.3β=0.3 it is −0.36-0.36−0.36. Each lies between the two values of −β-\beta−β, as the theory predicts. A latent coordinate counts as active when its encoder mean varies across test images with a variance above 0.010.010.01 (Burda, Grosse, and Salakhutdinov 2016). At β=100\beta = 100β=100 only 222 of the 888 coordinates stay active, and at β=30\beta = 30β=30 six of them do. Apart from the three repeated values, each β\betaβ was trained once. These models train for 101010 epochs against 303030 for the main 888-dimensional VAE, so their squared errors are not comparable with its 12.712.712.7.

Going furtherTighter bounds

Averaging KKK importance weights before the logarithm gives the importance weighted bound LK(x)=E[log⁡1K∑i=1Kpθ(x∣zi) p(zi)qϕ(zi∣x)]\mathcal{L}_K(x) = \mathbb{E}\big[\log \frac{1}{K} \sum_{i=1}^{K} \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z_i)\, p(z_i)}{q_\phi(z_i \mid x)}\big]LK​(x)=E[logK1​∑i=1K​qϕ​(zi​∣x)pθ​(x∣zi​)p(zi​)​], where z1,…,zKz_1, \dots, z_Kz1​,…,zK​ are drawn independently from the encoder (KKK counts samples, and kkk remains the latent dimension). The ELBO takes the logarithm of single weights and the log-likelihood is the logarithm of their expectation, and LK\mathcal{L}_KLK​ lies between the two. It satisfies log⁡pθ(x)≥LK+1≥LK\log p_\theta(x) \ge \mathcal{L}_{K+1} \ge \mathcal{L}_Klogpθ​(x)≥LK+1​≥LK​ with L1\mathcal{L}_1L1​ the ELBO, and it approaches log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) when the weights are bounded (Burda, Grosse, and Salakhutdinov 2016, Theorem 1). The estimate of the gap on MNIST above is LK\mathcal{L}_KLK​ with K=1,000K = 1{,}000K=1,000 minus the ELBO.

When it fails

We now have the formulas to explain what goes wrong. Each box below starts from what we see on trained models and traces it to what we have derived.

When it fails

Holes in the latent space

Of 1,0001{,}0001,000 codes drawn from the prior, 53%53\%53% decode into images that the shared classifier does not recognize with 90%90\%90% confidence, and for 14%14\%14% the confidence is below 50%50\%50%. Prior codes typically lie at distance about 8≈2.8\sqrt{8} \approx 2.88​≈2.8 from the origin, where 60,00060{,}00060,000 clouds of standard deviation 0.050.050.05 fill a negligible share of 888-dimensional space. The aggregate posterior differs from the prior, which by Corollary 16 costs KL(qˉϕ ∥ p)\mathrm{KL}(\bar{q}_\phi \,\|\, p)KL(qˉ​ϕ​∥p) nats per image, and prior codes land where the decoder has seen nothing. The clouds of the 222-dimensional model do fill the disk. Sampling codes from a second model fitted to the training codes replaces the prior by an estimate of qˉϕ\bar{q}_\phiqˉ​ϕ​.

When it fails

The code switches off

When the pull towards the prior weighs too much, or when the decoder is expressive enough to model images on its own (such as a decoder built like the autoregressive models of Chapter 1), the cheapest solution is qϕ(z∣x)=p(z)q_\phi(z \mid x) = p(z)qϕ​(z∣x)=p(z) for every image. The KL term then vanishes and the code carries no information about the image. This posterior collapse (Bowman et al. 2016) appears in the third column of the figure on the two terms of the loss, where 666 of the 888 coordinates are switched off.

The linear model gives the exact threshold. Its code uses a principal direction of the data only when the data vary along it more than the decoder noise, that is when the principal variance λj\lambda_jλj​ exceeds σdec2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}σdec2​ (Proposition 17). By Proposition 11 a weight β\betaβ on the KL term raises the threshold to βσdec2\beta\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}βσdec2​. Applied to the principal variances of MNIST, the rule roughly predicts when a nonlinear VAE starts to switch coordinates off. The test uses the VAEs of the rate-distortion box above, trained for 101010 epochs at seven values of β\betaβ from 0.10.10.1 to 100100100.

β\betaβ threshold βσdec2\beta\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}βσdec2​ number of principal directions above it (of 784784784) active coordinates predicted (of 888) active coordinates measured (of 888)
10 0.3 35 8 8
30 0.9 13 8 6
100 3.0 3 3 2

The code has only 888 coordinates, so the prediction stops at 888. The largest principal variances of MNIST are 5.15.15.1, 3.73.73.7 and 3.33.33.3, out of a total of 52.752.752.7. Up to β=10\beta = 10β=10 all 888 coordinates stay active, as predicted. At β=30\beta = 30β=30 and 100100100 the nonlinear model trained for 101010 epochs switches coordinates off a little earlier than the linear rule allows, at the same order of β\betaβ. I expected the linear rule to say little about a nonlinear network trained for only 101010 epochs. It gets the order of β\betaβ right.

When it fails

Mass between the modes

The VAE finds all 888 modes, but only 61.5%61.5\%61.5% of its samples land within three standard deviations of a mode, against 99.1%99.1\%99.1% for real data. Some bridge between the modes must exist, because a continuous decoder fed with a connected prior has a connected image. Prior codes that fall between the clusters of training codes decode onto the bridges. The forward KL of Chapter 2 averages over the data, so model mass where there are no data costs nothing directly and only leaves less mass for the modes. The decoder noise (σdec≈0.03\sigma_{\text{dec}} \approx 0.03σdec​≈0.03) is also wider than the modes (0.020.020.02), so the noisy model cannot resolve them exactly.

Where the blur comes from

Chapter 1 listed blurry samples as the cost of the VAE, and the latent explorer shows where they start. The codes between the cloud of the 7s and the cloud of the 9s decode into images that look like both. Several training images share each of these codes, and the decoder must answer one image for all of them. With the squared error of the Gaussian decoder, its best answer is their average.

Proposition 18 (The best decoder is a conditional mean). Fix the encoder, draw X∼P∗X \sim \mathbb{P}^*X∼P∗ and Z∼qϕ(⋅∣X)Z \sim q_\phi(\cdot \mid X)Z∼qϕ​(⋅∣X), and assume E∥X∥2<∞\mathbb{E}\|X\|^2 < \inftyE∥X∥2<∞. Among all functions g:Rk→Rdg : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^dg:Rk→Rd, the expected squared error E∥X−g(Z)∥2\mathbb{E}\|X - g(Z)\|^2E∥X−g(Z)∥2 is minimized by the conditional mean g∗(z)=E[X∣Z=z]g^*(z) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z = z]g∗(z)=E[X∣Z=z]. The minimum is E∥X−E[X∣Z]∥2\mathbb{E}\|X - \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z]\|^2E∥X−E[X∣Z]∥2, the average conditional variance of the images that share a code.

Proof.

Write g∗(Z)=E[X∣Z]g^*(Z) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z]g∗(Z)=E[X∣Z] and expand around it, E∥X−g(Z)∥2=E∥X−g∗(Z)∥2+2 E[(X−g∗(Z))⊤(g∗(Z)−g(Z))]+E∥g∗(Z)−g(Z)∥2. \mathbb{E}\|X - g(Z)\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\|X - g^*(Z)\|^2 + 2\, \mathbb{E}\big[(X - g^*(Z))^\top (g^*(Z) - g(Z))\big] + \mathbb{E}\|g^*(Z) - g(Z)\|^2 . E∥X−g(Z)∥2=E∥X−g∗(Z)∥2+2E[(X−g∗(Z))⊤(g∗(Z)−g(Z))]+E∥g∗(Z)−g(Z)∥2. In the middle term, condition on ZZZ. The vector g∗(Z)−g(Z)g^*(Z) - g(Z)g∗(Z)−g(Z) is then fixed and E[X−g∗(Z)∣Z]=0\mathbb{E}[X - g^*(Z) \mid Z] = 0E[X−g∗(Z)∣Z]=0, so the middle term is 000 by the tower property. The last term is non-negative and vanishes for g=g∗g = g^*g=g∗, which gives both claims.

The conditional mean is an explicit average of images. A code zzz is reached by the clouds of many images, and E[X∣Z=z]=EX∼P∗[X qϕ(z∣X)]qˉϕ(z), \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z = z] = \frac{\mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mathbb{P}^*}\big[X\, q_\phi(z \mid X)\big]}{\bar{q}_\phi(z)}, E[X∣Z=z]=qˉ​ϕ​(z)EX∼P∗​[Xqϕ​(z∣X)]​, the average of the images weighted by how strongly their clouds reach zzz, divided by the aggregate posterior of Proposition 15.

So blur comes from averaging, and averaging needs several images to share a code. Two things make them share one. An 888-number code cannot tell apart images that differ only in details it has no room for, and the KL penalty makes the encoder clouds overlap. Noise on the displayed images plays no part, since we show decoder means. The decoder variance enters only through the weight of the KL term.

We can measure how much of the blur the KL term causes. We score blur by the share of an image’s spectral power above a quarter cycle per pixel, where strokes have their edges. It is 10.5%10.5\%10.5% for real test digits and 4.7%4.7\%4.7% for the reconstructions of our VAE. I expected halving the KL weight to make the reconstructions sharper, since the clouds would overlap less. The VAE trained with the best decoder variance, which weighs the KL term about half as much, scores 4.9%4.9\%4.9%, so the share barely moved. The plain autoencoder of the same size has no KL term and no noise on its code. It scores 4.4%4.4\%4.4%, so its reconstructions are no sharper. It was trained for only 202020 epochs against 303030 for the VAEs, so this comparison is not clean. Only a much heavier penalty changes the picture. With the KL term weighted 100100100 times more, the share falls to 0.15%0.15\%0.15%. Each of these models was trained once, so the small differences between them may be noise.

So at our settings the KL term does not look like the main cause of the blur. That leaves the 888-number code, whose length we did not vary, and the squared-error loss.

This measure has a limit. A higher share does not always mean a better image, because artefacts carry high frequencies too. Prior samples score higher than reconstructions, 5.6%5.6\%5.6% against 4.7%4.7\%4.7% for our VAE, and the prior samples of the plain autoencoder score 4.9%4.9\%4.9% although almost none of them are digits.

Diffusion models (Chapter 7) are built on the fact behind this section, that a regression predicts a conditional average.

Going furtherExtensions

A conditional VAE (Sohn, Lee, and Yan 2015) lets the encoder and the decoder see the label. We then choose the digit, and the code describes its style. A VQ-VAE (Oord, Vinyals, and Kavukcuoglu 2017) uses discrete codes. Its encoder sends an image to the nearest vector of a learned dictionary, as k-means does. The k-means algorithm is itself an autoencoder whose code is the index of a cluster and whose decoder returns the cluster’s centre. A second model then learns to sample the indices, and the samples are less blurry. Latent diffusion (Rombach et al. 2022), the subject of Chapter 9, compresses images with an autoencoder that has a light KL penalty and generates in its latent space with a diffusion model.

Check yourself

  1. Why not maximize log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) directly?

    Answer

    It is an integral of a neural network over the whole latent space with no closed form, and estimating it by sampling the prior needs a number of codes that grows geometrically with kkk (Proposition 5). The ELBO replaces it by an expectation under the encoder that we can estimate and differentiate from single codes.

  2. What is the ELBO when qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z \mid x)qϕ​(z∣x) is the prior for every xxx?

    Answer

    The KL term is 000, so the ELBO is Ez∼p(z)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)]Ez∼p(z)​[logpθ​(x∣z)], the lower bound of Proposition 3. The code carries no information about xxx, and the best decoder maps every code to the mean image. This is posterior collapse.

  3. Doubling σdec2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}σdec2​ has the same minimizers as which β\betaβ?

    Answer

    β=2\beta = 2β=2, by Proposition 11. The loss 12⋅2σdec2∥x−g(z)∥2+KL\frac{1}{2 \cdot 2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}} \|x - g(z)\|^2 + \mathrm{KL}2⋅2σdec2​1​∥x−g(z)∥2+KL is half of 12σdec2∥x−g(z)∥2+2 KL\frac{1}{2\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}} \|x - g(z)\|^2 + 2\, \mathrm{KL}2σdec2​1​∥x−g(z)∥2+2KL.

  4. A linear VAE with k=1k = 1k=1 and σdec2=0.03\sigma^2_{\text{dec}} = 0.03σdec2​=0.03 is trained on MNIST, whose largest principal variance is 5.15.15.1. From which weight β\betaβ on the KL term does its code switch off?

    Answer

    By Proposition 17 and Proposition 11 the code is used while 5.1>0.03 β5.1 > 0.03\, \beta5.1>0.03β, so it switches off for β≥5.1/0.03\beta \ge 5.1 / 0.03β≥5.1/0.03, about 170170170.

  5. A VAE is trained with the prior N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I). Which prior would give it a higher average ELBO without retraining?

    Answer

    The aggregate posterior qˉϕ\bar{q}_\phiqˉ​ϕ​, the distribution of the codes of the training images (Corollary 16). The gain is KL(qˉϕ ∥ N(0,I))\mathrm{KL}(\bar{q}_\phi \,\|\, \mathcal{N}(0, I))KL(qˉ​ϕ​∥N(0,I)) nats per image.

  6. The importance weights of the encoder vary by a factor of hundreds on MNIST. Why is one code per image still enough to train?

    Answer

    The loss uses the logarithm of the weight, whose standard deviation is 6.76.76.7 nats. The single-code estimate is unbiased for the ELBO, and its noise averages out over the minibatch and the steps.

Summary

We began by hoping that the decoder of an autoencoder would generate, and with 0.3%0.3\%0.3% of its prior samples recognized as digits it did not, because nothing controlled where its codes lay. Replacing each code by a Gaussian cloud and pulling the clouds towards the prior raised the share to 47%47\%47%. At that stage these were two repairs with no theory behind them.

The theory came from asking for a likelihood. Gaussian noise on the decoder gives the generator a density, but one that is an integral over codes. Sampling that integral from the prior fails badly, and sampling it from the encoder works better, although the weights still vary a lot and the estimate of the likelihood stays poor. Taking the logarithm before averaging gives the evidence lower bound, which falls short of the log-likelihood by the KL from the encoder to the posterior. Averaged over the data, the negative bound equals KL(P∗ ∥ Pθ)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^* \,\|\, \mathbb{P}_\theta)KL(P∗∥Pθ​) plus that gap, up to a constant, so it is an upper bound on the distance. The gap is at least about 141414 nats for the median MNIST digit. Split in two, the bound gives back our two repairs, and the decoder variance sets their balance. The reparameterization trick then trains it from one code per image.

The failures can be read off the same formulas. The codes of the data do not fill the prior, whose best replacement is the aggregate posterior. In the linear model the code switches off along directions whose data variance is below βσdec2\beta\sigma^2_{\text{dec}}βσdec2​, and the nonlinear VAE follows this rule roughly. The squared-error decoder outputs the average of the images that share a code, which makes the samples blurry. Halving the KL weight or removing it did not sharpen the reconstructions, so at our settings it does not look like the main cause.

Chapter 4 trains a generator without a likelihood. A generative adversarial network trains the generator against a second network that learns to tell real images from generated ones. It needs no density and no decoder noise, and its samples are sharp. Its surrogate is a lower bound, and Chapter 2’s proposition on surrogates showed that training can exploit the gap of a lower bound.
